summary: Upper-KS2 learners (ages 9–11) build an understanding of the respiratory system as a pump-and-exchange system, keeping two strands distinct: (1) the AIR PATHWAY branching like an upside-down tree (nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli) and (2) the MECHANICS of how air is moved (the diaphragm, a muscle sheet below the lungs, contracts and flattens to enlarge the chest so the pressure inside drops and outside air is pushed in, then relaxes and domes up so the space shrinks and air flows out). The payoff is at the alveoli, where huge combined surface area and one-cell-thick walls wrapped in capillaries let oxygen cross into the blood and carbon dioxide cross out. Keep 'how air gets in' (diaphragm) separate from 'what the air is for' (exchange), because children routinely merge the two or think the lungs inflate themselves.
misconceptions: 'Lungs inflate themselves / the chest muscles just squeeze' — missing that the diaphragm below the lungs is the main driver, changing chest volume so air is pushed in by pressure.

'We breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide' as if the air swaps completely — in reality it is the same air mixture; only some oxygen is absorbed and some carbon dioxide added (carried from the KS1 breathing misconception).
'Air goes to the lungs and just sits there' — missing that the point is exchange with the blood at the alveoli.
'The lungs are two empty balloons' — missing the dense branching structure ending in millions of tiny sacs.
'Alveoli are the same as the tubes' — not distinguishing the delivery pipes (bronchioles) from the exchange sacs (alveoli).
'Air is pulled in by the nose sucking' — locating the pump in the wrong place; the driver is the diaphragm and chest volume.

activities.title: Drive the breathing pump
steps: Operate a model where you pull the diaphragm sheet down and watch air stream in through the branching trachea → bronchi → bronchioles and fill the alveoli; release it and watch the diaphragm dome up and air flow out.
Say aloud, for each move, whether the chest space is getting bigger or smaller, and whether air is going in or out.
Explain in your own words why air rushes IN when the space gets bigger (pressure inside drops below the outside air, which pushes in), not because the lungs pull it in by themselves.
Optionally feel this on your own body: place hands on your belly and notice it push outward as you breathe in.
activities.insight: YOU cause the breath by moving a muscle BELOW the lungs, which enlarges the chest volume so the pressure inside drops and outside air is pushed in — the lungs do not inflate themselves.

activities.title: Zoom into a single alveolus
steps: Look closely at one air sac wrapped in a red capillary and trace what happens to each gas: oxygen crosses the thin wall out of the air and into the blood; carbon dioxide crosses the other way out of the blood and into the air.
Explain where the oxygen goes NEXT — the blood carries it onward to the body.
Answer: if the sac walls were thick instead of extremely thin (far thinner than paper), why would that make getting oxygen into the blood harder?
activities.insight: Exchange is a two-way swap across very thin walls (the alveolus wall and the capillary wall are each only one cell thick) — not a one-way 'breathing in oxygen', and the air is only partly traded, not fully swapped. The point of reaching the alveoli is exchange with the blood.

activities.title: Trace and name the airway tree
steps: Trace the journey a single breath takes, naming each part in order as the tubes narrow and finally end in sacs: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
Drill down from an 'alveoli cluster' into a single alveolus-and-capillary to see where the pipes end and the exchange sacs begin.

Explain why the lungs branch into millions of tiny sacs rather than being two big empty bags, using a surface-area idea (spread flat, the sacs would cover a very large area, often estimated at around 50–100 square metres, roughly half a tennis court).
Point to the difference between the delivery pipes (bronchioles) and the exchange sacs (alveoli).
activities.insight: The airways form a branching tree ending in millions of tiny sacs; their huge combined surface area in a small space is a key reason gas exchange is so efficient (along with very thin walls and a rich blood supply), and the sacs are different from the pipes that deliver air to them.

activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, direction, and mechanism
steps: Put the airway stages in the correct order from nose/mouth to alveoli.
Match each part to its job (diaphragm → drives breathing; alveoli → gas exchange; bronchioles → delivery pipes).
Sort statements into 'breathing in' vs 'breathing out' (diaphragm contracts/flattens, space bigger, air in — vs relaxes/domes, space smaller, air out).
Decide, for a 'what happens at the alveoli' question, which description shows oxygen crossing into the blood rather than merely filling the lungs.
activities.insight: The pathway order, the diaphragm in/out mechanism, and the exchange direction can be recalled and distinguished once the model has built the underlying intuition.

checkQuestion: Air isn't pumped into your lungs the way the heart pumps blood — yet air still rushes in when you breathe in. What actually makes the air go IN? And once air reaches the tiny air sacs deep in the lungs, what happens to the oxygen — where does it go next, and how?
checkAnswer: The diaphragm (with the rib muscles) contracts and moves down and out, making the chest space bigger; this lowers the air pressure inside the lungs, so air rushes in from outside to fill the space. Breathing out is the reverse — the diaphragm relaxes, the space shrinks, air is pushed out. At the alveoli, oxygen passes through the thin walls into the blood in the capillaries, and carbon dioxide passes the other way out of the blood; the blood then carries the oxygen to the body.
